newsitem.title: LEBANON: Syria supporters dominate new Lebanese parliament.
newsitem.headline: Syria supporters dominate new Lebanese parliament.

text.p: After weeks of manoeuvring, occasionally chaotic voting and frequent charges of fraud Lebanon ended up on Tuesday with a new parliament that analysts say is just as subservient to Syria as the outgoing one.

As results came in from the final round of voting in the eastern Bekaa Valley, supporters of the pro-Syrian government emerged comfortably in control of the 128-member house, with the number of opposition deputies reduced to seven from 12.

Billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri, who won a Beirut seat at his first attempt and swept home with a bloc of more than 20 supporters, appeared the big winner in the five-week election, confirming his position as Lebanon's most powerful political figure.

But analysts said Hariri's triumph was more apparent than real because he failed to keep out three strong Beirut opponents he had vowed to defeat and because he was still not strong enough to dominate parliament.

He will still have to horse-trade with other political leaders who are also backed by Syria, particularly his arch-rival Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, in order to get his ambitious reconstruction projects approved.

"Hariri has more power in parliament, but the big picture is still the same. He still needs the others and he will have to horse-trade. He can't push things through parliament," Paul Salem, head of a Beirut think-tank, told Reuters.

Election alliances between Hariri, Berri and other powerful leaders were likely to prove ephemeral now that the voting was over, and the power struggles of the old parliament would resume soon, analysts said.

"Normal play will resume, especially when it comes to forming the new governmemnt, with Hariri, Berri and (President Elias) Hrawi fighting for posts," said Sarkis Naoum, a political columnist with the conservative Beirut daily an-Nahar.
A big change in the new parliament is that Moslem fundamentalists have dropped from 16 deputies and supporters to 10.
Sunni radical groups lost three of their four seats while the Shi'ite Hizbollah (Party of God) retained nine deputies and supporters from 12 at the last elections in 1992.

"The Sunni fundamentalists had their wings clipped strongly, which is not bad for the country," said a Beirut analyst who believed most aspects of the election were carefully manipulated by Syria, which has 35,000 troops in the country.
Hizbollah's wings were only slightly clipped because Syria needs its guerrillas to fight Israeli forces in south Lebanon, the analyst said.
"But Hizbollah got the big message that in Lebanon only Syria decides and you have only one sponsor -- Damascus not Tehran," he said.

Syria made the point after Iranian Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Vellayati came to Lebanon earlier this year and said the pro-Iranian group would win more seats in the election because of popularity it gained during Israel's massive bombardment of Lebanon in April.
Christian opposition candidates also found the elections hard going, although many Christian voters ignored calls to repeat a boycott they staged in 1992.
But the small handful who won was more than in 1992 when there were no opposition candidates at all.

"This parliament is starting with an opposition, which the 1992 parliament did not have," Salem said. He expected some candidates who won on pro-government lists to move into opposition later, as happened after 1992.
"In 1992 no opposition ran, so parliament was completely docile and the mood was more fearful. This time outspoken opposition candidates ran and made it or nearly made it," Salem said.

Salem, secretary-general of LADE, the Lebanese Association for the Democracy of Elections, the first independent group to monitor a Lebanese election, said the widespread abuses LADE reported probably affected the results of 10-15 candidates.
"Even without frauds the government lists would have got big majorities because they were massive coalitions of very powerful interests and leaders, and parties backed by Syria," he said.
"But the body of vocal opposition leaders would have been larger, although still small."
